sections.overview: The grey seal is a large North Atlantic mammal that hunts at sea and returns ashore to rest and breed. Its name means “hook-nosed sea pig,” describing the male’s arched muzzle.
sections.identification: As a true seal, it has no external ear flaps and cannot turn its hind flippers forward to walk; on land it moves in a caterpillar-like undulation. Adult females commonly reach about 2.0–2.3 metres and 150–200 kilograms, while large males can exceed 2.3 metres and 300 kilograms. Females are usually lighter silver-grey or brown with dark spots; males tend to be darker, with a longer muzzle and pale patches. A thick blubber layer insulates the body and stores energy.
sections.habitat: It ranges along temperate and subarctic North Atlantic coasts, especially off Canada and north-western Europe. It rests and breeds on islands, reefs, sandbanks, rocky beaches and, in some regions, seasonal ice. The Baltic population is distinct from the eastern North Atlantic group.
sections.diet: It catches fish near the seabed and in open water, especially sandeels, cod-family fish and flatfish, but also squid, octopus and some crustaceans. The local menu shifts with season and prey availability; adults may eat several kilograms daily, depending on body size and the energy content of their prey.
sections.behavior: The foreflippers steer while the hind flippers propel the seal underwater. The species has been recorded diving to about 475 metres and remaining submerged for nearly an hour; these are upper reported capacities, not every hunt. At Sable Island, playback experiments showed that mothers distinguished their own pup’s call; at Isle of May, playback tests found no detectable discrimination, revealing variation between populations.
sections.reproduction: After mating, a dormant embryo delays uterine implantation for about three months, timing birth for the following breeding season. Births fall in autumn in much of the eastern Atlantic, winter in the west and late winter in the Baltic. A female usually gives birth to one white-coated pup and nurses it for about two to three weeks on energy-rich milk. On studied Atlantic breeding grounds, mothers fast during lactation and use stored reserves; after weaning they return to sea. Females often return to familiar colonies, where dominant males may mate with several females. The pup sheds its lanugo near weaning and remains ashore while it matures before entering the sea without further maternal care. At Isle of May, pups can fast ashore for several weeks after weaning; timing varies among colonies.
sections.ecology: Grey seals alternate feeding trips with visits ashore to rest, moult and breed, sometimes travelling far offshore before returning to familiar areas. Their fish consumption links them to marine food webs and fisheries. Some North Sea porpoise carcasses show injuries judged consistent with grey seal predation, although its frequency remains uncertain.
sections.conservation: In the Baltic, hunting and pollution had sharply reduced grey seal numbers by the 1970s; the monitored population has since increased over several decades. HELCOM’s regional 2024 Red List assessment classed the population as Least Concern, but cites coastal development, fishing-gear entanglement and contaminants; warming could shift more pupping from ice onto land, where pup survival is lower, potentially affecting population growth. In U.S. waters, the species is protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, although vessel strikes and disturbance remain local concerns. HELCOM’s 2024 account also reports Least Concern for global IUCN status.
